Decision: in-process WebRTC with gortsplib v5 (RTSP pull) + pion v4, video re-packetized but not transcoded; WHEP-style signalling. Proven end to end on the test camera: headless Chrome decoded 1920x1080 @ 15 fps, 0 loss, first frame 1-2 s (keyframe wait), server 1-2% CPU / 24 MB. Key findings: camera RTSP is UDP-only (rejects RTP over TCP); real stream is H.264 Main 15 fps + G.711 A-law 16 kHz (ONVIF claims 30 fps / 8 kHz); camera packs SPS+PPS+IDR into one FU-A NAL with embedded Annex-B start codes, so raw RTP forwarding decodes 0 frames - fixed by decoding to access units and letting pion's payloader re-split. Wrote docs/cloud-redirect.md (static, app-side; camera trust decisions are in firmware, deferred). Per-connection verdicts: HTTP-tier services (registration, config, service discovery, P2P index, OTA metadata) likely impersonable pending the camera's TLS trust store, since no pinning exists app-side and request signing (HMAC-SHA1) proves client not server; answering service discovery also steers the P2P layer. P2P media/control session is the crux - opens with R1/R2 mutual certification (CertifyReq/Resp/Ack, RC5, RSA); impersonable only if keyed by device password/ID (which the owner has) vs a baked-in vendor key (unknown). Push is replaced not impersonated. Firmware download serveable but flashing depends on an image signature check. Key point: TianEye doesn't need to win P2P - it serves media over RTSP/ONVIF directly and only needs cloud P2P impersonated OR blocked. Open questions all require firmware (te-99x.12) or capture (te-2dc).

Wrote docs/local-storage.md (synthesis, doc-only). Per-data-type verdict: live video + continuous recordings = rebuild from camera via RTSP/ONVIF (PROVEN, already working); alarm snapshots = grab frame from stream on alarm (feasible) or receive camera upload (unknown, te-99x.10); cloud HLS recordings = not needed (own recording replaces); settings model = keep locally if control channel reachable; bindings = TianEye's own data; face/bird AI = can't copy vendor's server-side model, could run own detector (separate work); PTZ presets = positions on camera, names/thumbnails local; push = replace with own notifications. Bottom line: everything that matters is rebuildable from the camera's LAN interfaces, not copied from cloud; only vendor server-side AI and anything needing to win the P2P session are out, and neither blocks the core goal (RTSP/ONVIF suffice).

Appended the final verdict to docs/cloud-redirect.md. Verdict: yes, all China-bound traffic can be stopped - by BLOCKING, not impersonating. Recommended config: (1) firewall block all WAN egress for the camera (hard guarantee, catches hardcoded IPs and DoH); (2) local DNS answering vendor hostnames with TianEye so lookups fail fast / can be emulated; (3) allow only LAN RTSP/ONVIF plus a local NTP. Per-destination rule table (block all cloudlinks.cn/cloud-links.net, block public DNS/NTP, block hardcoded IPs by IP, block OTA). Blocking beats impersonating because it needs no knowledge of camera trust, is verifiable from firewall logs, and TianEye loses nothing (rebuilds video/recording/snapshots from LAN). Residual risk = unconfirmed camera behaviour with cloud blocked, the one must-test-on-hardware item (deferred te-2dc/te-99x.12).

Done: docs/protocol-iotvideo.md (transport layer). gute frame = 24-byte header (magic 0x7E/0x7F, type, uint16 total length, 8-byte id, body-prefix word, 32-bit XOR checksum, flags word) + payload. Flags decoded: zlib bit, encryption mode (0 none / 1 per-frame-key RC5 / 2 session-key RC5), reliability (ack) bits, response/skip-checksum, extended-header and detect bits. Checksum formula captured. Encryption is standard RC5-32 (canonical P/Q constants confirmed), 8-byte blocks, three key schedules (id / per-frame-derived / session); mode 1 is obfuscation since its key comes from the cleartext header. Fragment/detect XOR obfuscation noted. Transport: UDP v4/v6 direct/NAT/LAN or TCP relay, KCP for reliable streams. Open: live-capture confirmation (te-2dc), RC5 round count (te-qgj.4), KCP tuning.

Done: docs/protocol-iotvideo.md 'Session Setup'. Four stages mapped from native functions/strings: (1) service discovery GET /iotvideo/service/ListService/GetServiceList?serviceId&token returns Asrv (access server) and p2psrv (relay) lists with v4/v6 addrs; (2) register with Asrv (init-info/online msg + 35/40/50s heartbeats), signalling layer keyed {msg_id,tid,path,code,json}; (3) detect fastest p2psrv + CALLING_REQ to wake device + ListNat NAT exchange; (4) MTP session via add_lan_or_nat (LAN/P2P), add_udp_relay or add_tcp_relay (RELAY), matching ConnectionMode. Open: GetServiceList JSON, control-message byte layouts, and whether LAN session works with no servers (all need capture/te-qgj.4).

Done: docs/protocol-iotvideo.md 'Crypto and Certification'. Mechanism decoded: session holds RC5-32 schedules - hardcoded bootstrap key 'www.gwell.cc' (base64 d3d3Lmd3ZWxsLmNj, non-secret), a 16-byte per-device certify key at device-link+0x330, and a session key. CertifyReq (type 0x0C) sends a 32-byte random R1 encrypted with the certify key; on CertifyResp the session cipher is keyed from R1 directly (mode-2 RC5). RC5 is standard (canonical P/Q). Found a separate LAN-password check/modify path (iv_check_set_lan_device_pwd -> giot_eif_send_check/modify_lan_pwd) that may allow password-only LAN auth. CRUX UNRESOLVED: whether the +0x330 certify key is password-derived (TianEye can forge) or cloud-issued (cannot); +0x330 is written via a computed pointer, needs more tracing or a capture. Filed te-qgj.8 to resolve. crypto-and-auth.md and cloud-redirect.md cross-linked.

Done: docs/protocol-gwell.md. Legacy stack shares the gute frame family (RC5-32, XOR checksum), MTP/KCP transport (lan_or_nat/tcp_lan/udp_relay), service discovery /gwellcloud/service/ListService/GetServiceList, UDP 8899 LAN search, avctl_* AV control, 28-byte PTZ frame - all cross-referenced. KEY FINDING: legacy auth password is computable from the device password with no vendor secret - P2PEncryptGW1 = fold(MD5(pw)) into a uint32 (four 32-bit words mod 999999999 XOR a constant table), gated by IsNeedEncrypt (all-digit pws); fgP2PGetMD5PasswordWithSrc = hex MD5; gw_EncodePassword = keyless 17-round LCG. So TianEye can likely authenticate to legacy Gwell cameras with just the device password (unlike the IoTVideo crux). Certify uses RSA session-key exchange but the password check is the auth gate. RESOLVED: the IoTVideo certify key is derived from the cloud-issued ACCESS TOKEN, not the device password. iv_set_access_token hex-decodes the accessToken into a 64-byte blob at term+0x300 (decoded token starts with 0x02); the 16-byte certify key is at offset 0x30 (+0x330) and is re-keyed on every token set/refresh (iv_update_access_id_token). So completing the IoTVideo P2P handshake requires a valid cloud-issued token - the device password alone is insufficient. Verdict for IoTVideo stands: block the cloud, serve media over RTSP/ONVIF; do not impersonate P2P. Documented in protocol-iotvideo.md (crux RESOLVED), cloud-redirect.md, protocol-go-guide.md. Filed follow-up for the only remaining loophole (LAN-password path).
